claim.text: There exist trainable sparse sub-networks, termed "boosting tickets", that are obtained by magnitude-based pruning of a trained dense model and resetting the remaining weights to the original initialization mask.

When retrained in isolation, boosting tickets (as described in claim 1) converge significantly faster than both the original dense model and winning tickets (sub-networks that, when trained from their initialization, achieve test accuracy comparable to the full dense model).

Boosting tickets (as described in claim 1) achieve comparable final test accuracy to the dense model and to winning tickets (sub-networks that, when trained from their initialization, achieve test accuracy comparable to the full dense model).
The one-shot prune-and-retrain recipe described in note 1 yields boosting tickets with the accelerated convergence and matched final accuracy reported for multiple architectures.

Experiments on VGG-16 and ResNet-18 on CIFAR-10 show that iterative pruning (multiple train-prune-reset cycles) and one-shot pruning produce boosting tickets with overlapping validation accuracy over training epochs, indicating that the boosting effects and final accuracy are empirically indistinguishable.
Iterative pruning (multiple train-prune-reset cycles) is not necessary for obtaining boosting tickets.

The strength of the boosting effect is controlled primarily by three empirical factors: (A) pruning-time learning rate (tested values 0.005, 0.01, 0.05, 0.1; intermediate small values 0.01 for VGG-16 and 0.05 for ResNet-18 are optimal) — smaller pruning learning rates produce stronger boosting; (B) pruning ratio (80% used as standard) — pruning ratios in the range approximately 60%–90% yield the strongest early-epoch gains; (C) model capacity — larger width and depth increase boosting strength.
Small models (e.g., LeNet with two convolutional layers and two fully connected layers) do not exhibit winning or boosting behavior under large pruning ratios.
The lottery ticket hypothesis, as described in note 2, and the boosting-ticket phenomenon, as described in note 3, apply under adversarial training regimes.

Specifically, magnitude-pruned sub-networks obtained from dense models trained naturally, with Fast Gradient Sign Method (FGSM)-based adversarial training, or with Projected Gradient Descent (PGD)-based adversarial training, when retrained using PGD-based adversarial training , (a) achieve comparable clean accuracy and robust accuracy to the full dense model and (b) converge faster than randomly reinitialized sparse models.

The procedure described in note 4 (Ours-40, retrained for 40 epochs) yields test accuracies and robust accuracies comparable to or slightly better than the baseline full model trained with 100-epoch PGD-based adversarial training (Madry et al.'s method): natural accuracy 87.72% vs 86.21%; PGD-20 robust accuracy 50.37% vs 50.07%; PGD-100 robust accuracy 49.28% vs 49.32%; Carlini-Wagner (C&W) attack robust accuracy 50.92% vs 50.46%.

The total wall-clock time for Ours-40 (the procedure described in claim 11) is 69,552 seconds, which is 0.51 times the 134,764 seconds of the baseline described in claim 11, saving 49% of total training time while achieving comparable or better robustness on white-box PGD-20, PGD-100, C&W attacks and black-box transfer attacks from other models.

On VGG-16 and ResNet-18 trained on CIFAR-10 with 80% magnitude pruning and the one-shot procedure, one-shot magnitude-based pruning followed by reset-and-retrain yields boosting tickets whose validation accuracy over epochs and final test accuracy are empirically indistinguishable from the validation accuracy over epochs and final test accuracy obtained via iterative pruning.
Iterative pruning is not necessary to obtain boosting tickets in the experiments on VGG-16 and ResNet-18 trained on CIFAR-10 with 80% magnitude pruning and the one-shot procedure.

The empirical failure of prior work to find winning tickets under adversarial training (training via Projected Gradient Descent adversarial examples) on small architectures is explained by model capacity limits: small convolutional networks that are adequate for natural training become unstable when heavily pruned under adversarial training and can collapse to trivial classifiers (e.g., constant predictions), whereas larger architectures do exhibit winning tickets and boosting tickets (sub-networks matching full model accuracy) under adversarial training.

note.text: A practical procedure for obtaining boosting tickets consists of: (i) training a dense model once using a small learning rate (e.g., for VGG-16 use pruning learning rate 0.01; for ResNet-18 use 0.05), (ii) pruning a large fraction of weights by magnitude (commonly 80% of weights with smallest magnitude), producing a binary mask, (iii) applying the mask to the saved original initialization and retraining the masked sub-network using learning-rate warmup from the small training learning rate up to the usual training learning rate (e.g., VGG-16 warmup from 0.01 to 0.1; ResNet-18 warmup from 0.05 to 0.1).
(stating that a randomly initialized dense neural network contains a sub-network that, when trained in isolation from its initialization, matches the test accuracy of the original network)
(sub-networks that converge significantly faster than the original network and other winning tickets)

A practical two-stage workflow for obtaining a strongly robust model with reduced training time consists of: (i) training a dense WideResNet-34-10 model (46.16 million parameters) on CIFAR-10 with Fast Gradient Sign Method (FGSM)-based adversarial training (bound 8/255 in L∞ norm) to obtain a weakly robust model, (ii) pruning 80% of weights by magnitude and resetting the surviving weights to the original initialization to obtain a boosting ticket, (iii) retraining the boosting ticket with 10-step Projected Gradient Descent (PGD)-based adversarial training (step size 2/255, bound 8/255) to obtain a strongly robust model.
